questiontext.text: Which list correctly names the three kinds of variables discussed in class design?

generalfeedback.text: Fields, parameters, and local variables each serve a distinct purpose.

answer.text: Fields, parameters, and local variables

feedback.text: Correct — these are the three kinds emphasised.

answer.text: Fields, arrays, and constants

feedback.text: No — arrays/constants are separate concepts, not the three variable kinds here.

answer.text: Parameters, methods, and classes

feedback.text: Methods/classes aren’t variables.

answer.text: Locals, packages, and modules

feedback.text: Packages/modules are not variables.

questiontext.text: What are the scope and lifetime of a field?

generalfeedback.text: Fields belong to the object; they are visible throughout the class and live as long as the object exists.

answer.text: Scope: the whole class; Lifetime: the lifetime of the object

feedback.text: Correct — fields persist with the object and are accessible throughout the class.

answer.text: Scope: the declaring method; Lifetime: a single call

feedback.text: No — that description matches locals, not fields.

answer.text: Scope: package; Lifetime: until program exit

feedback.text: Package scope is not how fields work; their lifetime is tied to the object.

answer.text: Scope: a single block; Lifetime: one iteration

feedback.text: That describes a block-scoped local, not a field.

questiontext.text: What is the primary role of a parameter in a method or constructor?

generalfeedback.text: Parameters receive values from the caller to help perform the task.

answer.text: To receive values from outside so the method can do its work

feedback.text: Correct — a fresh set of parameter values is provided on each call.

answer.text: To persist data for the object across calls

feedback.text: No — that’s the job of fields, not parameters.

answer.text: To control visibility of fields

feedback.text: Visibility is set by access modifiers, not parameters.

answer.text: To print formatted output

feedback.text: Formatting is unrelated to the purpose of parameters.

generalfeedback.text: Execution stops immediately after a return statement; later statements are not executed.

answer.text: The return ends the method, so the assignment to zero never runs

feedback.text: Correct — code after the return is unreachable.

answer.text: Assignments are illegal after a comment

feedback.text: Comments do not affect legality of assignments.

answer.text: The method needs two return statements

feedback.text: The number of return statements is not the issue; order and reachability are.

answer.text: Only void methods may assign to fields

feedback.text: Non-void methods can assign to fields; that’s not the problem here.

questiontext.text: What is a typical use of a local variable inside a method?

generalfeedback.text: Locals are short-lived, for temporary calculation/storage within a method’s block.

answer.text: Temporary storage needed during the method’s execution

feedback.text: Correct — locals exist only while the method/block runs.

answer.text: Long-term storage across many method calls

feedback.text: That’s what fields are for, not locals.

answer.text: Receiving input from outside the method

feedback.text: That’s the job of parameters.

answer.text: Controlling public/private visibility

feedback.text: Visibility modifiers apply to members, not local variables.

generalfeedback.text: The local stores the value before balance is cleared, letting the method both clear and return the amount.

answer.text: To keep the amount while we reset the field, then return it

feedback.text: Correct — the local holds the original balance for the return.

answer.text: Because fields cannot be read in non-void methods

feedback.text: Fields can be read anywhere in the class.

answer.text: Because parameters cannot be declared in methods

feedback.text: Parameters are declared in method headers; this is a local.

answer.text: To avoid using return statements

feedback.text: The method still uses a return; the local doesn’t eliminate it.

questiontext.text: What is the scope of a local variable declared inside a method block?

generalfeedback.text: The scope of a local is the block in which it is declared (and nested inner blocks).

answer.text: The block in which it is declared

feedback.text: Correct — the local is not visible outside that block.

answer.text: The entire class

feedback.text: That describes fields, not locals.

answer.text: The whole package

feedback.text: Locals never have package-wide scope.

answer.text: Across all methods of the class

feedback.text: Locals are not shared across methods.

generalfeedback.text: A local’s lifetime is the time of execution of the block in which it is declared.

answer.text: Only while the containing block is executing

feedback.text: Correct — once the block finishes, the local is gone.

answer.text: For the lifetime of the object

feedback.text: That’s the lifetime of fields, not locals.

answer.text: Until program termination

feedback.text: Locals do not persist to program end.

answer.text: Across all future calls to the method

feedback.text: Each call gets fresh locals; they don’t persist across calls.

generalfeedback.text: Scope is a static (textual) region in the source; lifetime is a dynamic (runtime) period of existence.

answer.text: Scope: where the name is visible in the source; Lifetime: how long the variable exists at runtime

feedback.text: Correct — scope is textual; lifetime is temporal.

answer.text: Scope is runtime; lifetime is compile-time

feedback.text: It’s the other way around: scope is textual, lifetime is runtime.

answer.text: They are synonyms

feedback.text: No — they refer to different concepts.

answer.text: Scope applies only to classes; lifetime only to methods

feedback.text: Both concepts apply to many program elements.

questiontext.text: Why do local variables not use visibility modifiers like public or private?

generalfeedback.text: Locals are not members; their visibility is confined to their block by definition.

answer.text: Because their visibility is already limited to the declaring block

feedback.text: Correct — locals aren’t class members, so access modifiers don’t apply.

answer.text: Because Java doesn’t allow modifiers anywhere

feedback.text: Java allows modifiers for members; locals are a special case.

answer.text: Because locals are always public by default

feedback.text: Locals are not public; they are block-scoped.

answer.text: Because they are stored in a different file

feedback.text: Storage location is unrelated; the reason is block scope.
